reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its primary purpose is an instructional demonstration claiming that DoorDash credits can reduce the cost of later meals, with a checkout screen showing credits applied and a zero-dollar total. Although the described method involves submitting a possibly false missing-item report and creating another account if detected, it does not request viewers to send money, credentials, or payment to the speaker. The sensational title, Instagram-follow request, visible account credit, and referral option provide promotional or app context but do not establish a financial solicitation or a connection between social engagement and the credit process.

opening.argument: Judge, the promise is not merely that credits exist. The video advertises “free DoorDash for life,” then gives viewers a specific action to obtain credits: report an item missing even when it was not. The speaker says that submitting this claim makes DoorDash give them money toward later meals. That is an easy-reward solicitation tied to a deceptive claim, even though the money would come as app credit rather than a payment from the speaker.

But they will give you credit money. Going towards your next meals.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense's app-navigation quote does not make the instruction benign. The decisive step is telling viewers to claim an item is missing when it probably was not. Nor does the absence of a payment to the speaker answer the concern: the requested false claim is how viewers are told to get the promised credit.

citations.quote: Hit missing item. Even though you probably weren't missing items, hit it.
Go. And just. Act like you were missing shit. So then they have to give you money back.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The instruction to make a false report is explicit, but the video demonstrates a DoorDash support and credit workflow, not a separate claim site, paid enrollment, or transfer to the speaker. The speaker also says the claim will not always produce credit. These facts support treating the video as an operational tutorial about abusing an app process, without establishing that the video itself is a scam solicitation.

citations.quote: What you want to do is go to your DoorDash, click orders.
But look, sometimes it's not,. They won't do it.

opening.argument: Consider the signals together: an emphatic promise of free DoorDash “for life,” a concrete example of credits covering a later order, and instructions for what to do if the platform catches on. The speaker says to create a new account with a new phone number so the accounts will not be connected. That evasion advice makes the easy-credit pitch more concerning than an ordinary explanation of how refunds work.

If they end up catching on to it. All you have to do is make a new account.
so they won't connect the two accounts and then after that. You'll be fine.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense acknowledges both the false report and the replacement-account advice, but treats them as incidental to a demonstration. They are part of the proposed way to keep obtaining the benefit. A checkout example showing applied credit illustrates possible use of credit; it does not establish that the promised “for life” method is reliable or legitimate.

citations.quote: Act like you were missing shit. So then they have to give you money back.
If they end up catching on to it. All you have to do is make a new account.
FREE DOORDASH FOR LIFE

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The title overstates the method, and the account advice is troubling. But the speaker describes credits applied to future orders while admitting that DoorDash sometimes will not grant them. The evidence shows instruction in an abusive refund tactic, not a guaranteed reward flow or a request for viewers to give the speaker money or account details.

citations.quote: That $13.80 is going to cover $7 of that.
But look, sometimes it's not,. They won't do it.

opening.argument: The app walkthrough also works as a pitch for participation. The speaker first asks viewers to follow his Instagram, then presents the steps for obtaining credits and tells viewers to act as though an item was missing. He describes the resulting credit as covering food on a later order. The instructional format should not obscure the call to try the method: the promised benefit depends on viewers taking the deceptive action themselves.

citations.quote: But first, make sure y'all follow me on Instagram at k.boogie with five E's.

Go. And just. Act like you were missing shit. So then they have to give you money back.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that following Instagram is not presented as a condition for receiving DoorDash credit. But that does not reduce the video to neutral app instruction. The speaker directly tells viewers to report a missing item even when none was missing; the social-media request adds promotion without being the credit mechanism.

citations.quote: But first, make sure y'all follow me on Instagram at k.boogie with five E's.
Hit missing item. Even though you probably weren't missing items, hit it.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The Instagram request is separate from the credit steps: the speaker directs viewers to their own DoorDash order history and its Help option, not to an account or payment channel he controls. The false-report instruction is real and objectionable, but promotional tone and a call to try it do not by themselves change the primary content from a demonstration of app misuse into a scam solicitation.
